On Nov. 6, FDA will hold the second of its public meetings on what it calls[Challenges and Solutions in Lot-Level Food Traceability](https://www.fda.gov/food/workshops-meetings-webinars-food-and-dietary-supplements/fda-public-meeting-challenges-and-solutions-lot-level-food-traceability-11062026?ref=foodsafetynews.com). Anyone who wants to speak must [register by Oct. 26](https://www.fda.gov/food/workshops-meetings-webinars-food-and-dietary-supplements/fda-public-meeting-challenges-and-solutions-lot-level-food-traceability-11062026?ref=foodsafetynews.com), and no same-day registration is allowed.[Written comments are due Dec. 6](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/09/2026-20720/challenges-and-solutions-in-lot-level-food-traceability-public-meeting?ref=foodsafetynews.com)in Docket No. FDA-2014-N-0053. The meeting is billed as a chance to talk about implementation. Read the notice closely and it is something narrower: A conversation about how to make the rule’s core requirement, the lot code, easier to live without.

So here is where the Food Traceability Rule stands, how it got here, and why, more than fifteen years after Congress ordered it, FDA cannot spend a dollar enforcing a single line of it.
